title: EcoAct: Economic Agent Determines When to Register What Action

live_model.evidence: Table 1 (Comparison of ReAct with EcoAct on ToolBench): "GPT-4-turbo ReaAct 16.2 6.3 18.5 8.1 13.2 11.5 16.0 8.6" (Pass Rate %% and Cost cents per G1/G2/G3 subset and Average).

prompt.location: Sec 3.1/3.2 and Appendix A: agent reasoning follows the public ToolBench/ReAct prompting setup; pass-rate evaluation "applying the same prompts as those used in ToolBench"
prompt.note: Prompts are the established public ToolBench/ReAct templates plus the paper's own tool-name-registration meta-tool instruction (Sec. 2); not independently re-quoted verbatim in the main text.

claim.metric: pass rate (%), GPT-4-turbo backbone with vanilla ReAct (no EcoAct), Average across G1-G3
claim.location: Table 1, row 'GPT-4-turbo ReaAct', Average PR column; n from the six filtered ToolBench subsets used in the paper (115+132+142+107+98+38=632 queries, Sec 3.1)

data.source: ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023), filtered per AnyTool (Du et al. 2024); https://github.com/gkamradt/LLMTest_NeedleInAHaystack referenced for a related probe

notes: GPT-4-turbo is one of two backbone LLMs (with GPT-4o) run as the ReAct tool-use agent on ToolBench, both with and without the paper's EcoAct tool-registration method; GPT-4-turbo is also separately used as the pass-rate judge (self-judging its own ReAct runs, applying ToolBench's standard evaluation prompts). Cost is agentic (multiple tool-call rounds per query), so likely several thousand calls across 632 queries -- high tier even at gpt-4-turbo's per-call price.
